source.lineage: Formulated around 1998-2004 by Steve Roden in Los Angeles, Bernhard Gunter in Germany and Richard Chartier and the 12k and Line labels in New York — extreme-quiet composition built from close-miked microsound (paper, water, insects, small objects) and digital silence, presented near the noise floor at levels that force the listener to raise playback volume, with long silences, no beat, no harmony and near-total absence of dynamic gesture.

extras.description: Lowercase is a turn-of-the-millennium practice named by Steve Roden in which amplified, close-miked micro-events and digital near-silence become the entire material of a piece. It is distinguished from dark ambient and isolationism by its refusal of drone mass and low-end weight, and from glitch by using acoustic microsound and silence rather than digital error as its rhetoric.

source.lineage: Tokyo improvised-music movement crystallized around the Off Site venue circa 1998-2004 and codified by Otomo Yoshihide, Sachiko M, Toshimaru Nakamura and Taku Sugimoto — extremely quiet, near-static music of sine tones, no-input mixing-board feedback, contact-mic scrapes and long silences, with no pulse, no harmony and structure emerging from the acoustics of the room itself.

extras.description: Onkyokei emerged in Tokyo's small improvisation venues around 1998, most associated with the Off Site space in Yoyogi. It differs from European free improvisation in its refusal of gesture and virtuosity, and from ambient music in that it is performed live, unlooped and without harmonic bed.

source.name: Caucasian Folk Music (Regional Composite)
source.lineage: Regional composite of the mountain traditions between the Black and Caspian seas, recorded ethnographically from wax cylinder in the 1900s through Melodiya's Soviet republic series, characterized by drone-anchored vocal polyphony in Georgia, narrow-range modal solo song and lament in Armenia and Dagestan, double-reed and accordion dance music in fast 6/8 at 130-180 BPM, and heterophonic plucked and bowed accompaniment on panduri, tar and kamancha with frame and cylinder drums.

extras.description: An umbrella category for the village musics of the Caucasus isthmus, spanning Georgian, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Dagestani, Chechen and Circassian practice as documented by Russian and Soviet ethnographers from the 1900s onward. Common threads are drone-based rather than chordal accompaniment, non-tempered modal intonation, sharply metered 6/8 dance repertoire alongside unmeasured lament, and outdoor double-reed-and-drum ensembles for weddings. It is broader than any single national tradition here and should be treated as the shared substrate from which Georgian polyphony, Armenian folk and lezginka each specialize.

source.name: Ambient synth
source.lineage: Synthesizer-led ambient in which articulated patterns and changing electronic timbres remain recognizable, represented by Steve Hauschildt’s solo work around Strands (2016). A harmonic bed can give rise to arpeggios and aleatoric sequences, then be shaped through processing and editing. This selected pattern-oriented branch differs from beatless, steady-state space ambient and from the historically specific Berlin School.

extras.description: Ambient synth centers the synthesizer as a played or programmed sound source: slowly changing harmony, gently articulated figures and interacting electronic voices create the space without requiring drums or acoustic instruments. The selected Hauschildt branch combines arpeggiated motion with flexible timing and detailed processing, rather than treating every synth part as an undifferentiated drone. The default pairs a soft short-envelope triangle figure with harmonic FM tones; these are authored ways to achieve the sourced practice, not claims about Strands’ instruments. Unlike space ambient, repeated note attacks remain a compositional foreground; unlike Berlin School, neither a 1970s tape ensemble nor a fixed ostinato defines the scope.
exemplars: Steve Hauschildt — Where All Is Fled (2015)
